McCall's 5795 Girl's Dress Sewing Pattern Review

My daughter really enjoys the dresses that I sew for her, usually for Easter and Birthday presents every year. Her birthday is coming up soon, and I have 3 new patterns and a bunch of cute cotton prints in my fabric stash; so this is 1 of 3 dresses that she is receiving for her 10th birthday this year. The dresses aren't a surprise, so I'm giving them to her as they are finished. She is particular and requested short sleeves and calf-length skirts.

My kid is 4'9" and 69 lbs. Her measurements are: chest 26", waist 24", hip 27", so I used the size 10 dress pattern which had a couple inches of ease. It fits her nicely with a couple inches to grow into. The back length was 39" by pattern (exactly what she wanted), so I didn't have to change the hem.

Changes: I used an invisible zipper. I made view D with a contrasting fabric sash. I serged the bodice to the skirt.

A beginner could sew this pattern, but I do think a more advanced sewer would more "smartly" sew the bodice part of the pattern. The instructions call for some unnecessary sewing, flipping, understitching: I don't know why they made it so complicated. My advice:

  • Sew the bodice darts on main and lining

  • Sew the main front and back together at the shoulders, and same for lining

  • Right sides together, sew the neck edge of main and lining together

  • Press and understitch neck edge

  • Sew front and back side edges together on main, and same for lining; press seams

  • Baste raw armhole edges together

  • Assemble sleeves, according to instructions, press up 5/8" on sleeve lining armhole edge

  • Sew main sleeve to the bodice, slipstitch the pressed sleeve lining in place

With that method, it's just simpler to have a nicely finished bodice on the inside. Or if you didn't mind some overlocked seams along the armpits, you could skip the last two points and just serge the sleeves on.

This dress was really easy to make. It only took me a few hours. When I was finishing up the skirt, I had my daughter work on the sash. She sewed it together, flipped it right-side out, ironed it. I got her started on the top-stitching (which I think is sort of essential for little girls' sashes to stay neat and not all bunched up like a rope) with my 1/4" foot, and she finished the rest of the top-stitching. Her extra birthday gift there was learning some sewing skills! I know it is all too easy to have that seamstress Mom sew everything and the daughter miraculously never learn how to sew herself--but I do want to prevent that if I can. I want to pass on the sewing skills to the next generation.
